# StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue

Samarth Varshney    Ritu Yadav

###### Abstract

Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up
front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and
return. Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) degrade in this
regime in two ways—active constraints stop being honored as turns
accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being
enacted (relapse)—and the only existing repair we are aware of is an
external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification at every turn.
To tackle this, we propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that
teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state. We
formalize evolving-constraint dialogue as edit trajectories over a typed
state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so that persistence and
relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are
compiled for free. StateWise first fine-tunes the LLM on two
complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state
and responding conditioned on that state; it then self-trains on
trajectories the model itself generates, keeping only turns that pass an
exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This recipe teaches
7–8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not
to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles
relapse, and on Qwen2.5-7B none reduces it. We therefore add a
preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, in which the
rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen response passes
the round-trip check. Experiments on two backbones with held-out
constraint families and unseen phrasings show that StateWise cuts
relapse by 8–22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts
conversation success by 8–19 points over the backbone, and beats an
oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time
scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe’s cost on
cumulative-constraint and single-turn benchmarks and study weight
interpolation as a mitigation.

## 1 Introduction

Conversational assistants are asked to follow instructions that evolve.
A user asks for a summary in bullet points, then wants it under a
hundred words, then drops the bullets, digresses to an unrelated
question, and returns to the summary expecting the word limit to still
hold and the bullets to be gone. Multi-turn instruction following is now
benchmarked at scale: Multi-IF ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)) extends
IFEval ([Zhou et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)) to three turns and finds
accuracy falling with every turn; SysBench ([Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)) measures the instability of system-message adherence;
EvolIF ([Jia et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)) constructs evolving dialogues
with constraint changes and reports deficiencies in failure recovery. A
parallel line isolates a specific pathology: when a user withdraws a
constraint, the model often keeps enacting it, a failure that ReBIND
([Zhu, 2026](#bib.bib19)) names _revocation inertia_ and shows rising
from 0.01 to 0.40 for an 8B model as the constraint load grows.

Training-side work has addressed adjacent problems. Reinforcement
learning with verifiable rewards improves single-turn multi-constraint
following ([Pyatkin et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)); label-free variants
derive rewards from the instructions themselves ([Ren et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)); curriculum RL with abstention rewards mitigates the
lost-in-conversation gap for information revealed across turns ([Laban
et al., 2026](#bib.bib5); [Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). None of these
trains the model to hold a _revisable_ constraint state across edits. To
our knowledge the only published repair for relapse is inference-time:
ReBIND keeps an external ledger with tombstones and compiles the net
specification into every request, at roughly $`1.5\times`$ delivery cost
and only for code.

We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single
LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state. Our design follows a
recipe proven effective for label-free domain adaptation: SimRAG ([Xu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)) fine-tunes one LLM on complementary skills,
uses the same model to synthesize training data, and keeps only examples
that survive a round-trip consistency check. StateWise transposes this
recipe to evolving-constraint dialogue. The complementary skills are
constraint-state summarization and state-conditioned response
generation; the unlabeled resource is single-turn verifiable
constraints, which we compose into scripted add/amend/revoke
trajectories; and the round-trip check is exact equality between the
model’s emitted state and the compiled ground truth, together with
executable checkers and a relapse guard. Because the state is compiled
from the edit history, every training signal and metric in this paper is
verifiable without human annotation.

The recipe teaches the state and, surprisingly, fails to teach obedience
to it. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct the self-improved model emits the
correct state, including the correct tombstones, for 92% of
in-distribution turns, and then enacts the revoked rule anyway at more
than twice the backbone’s rate. On Llama the same doubling of relapse
appears in every supervised variant we trained, with or without state
supervision, and even single-turn constraint training raises relapse:
making a model better at obeying constraints makes withdrawn constraints
stickier. Rejection-sampling SFT removes relapsed examples from the
training set but supplies no signal _against_ relapse. We therefore add
a second self-improvement stage that turns the round-trip check into a
preference signal: the model’s own relapsed generations become rejected
responses, its round-trip-clean generations become chosen responses, and
a short DPO run on these self-labeled contrasts cuts relapse by 8–22
points, to below the backbone and below an oracle compiled-ledger
system, on two backbones, two training seeds and unseen phrasings.
Ablations show that the relapse-specific contrast is necessary
(preference pairs about active constraints alone _raise_ relapse) and
that label-shuffled pairs do nothing, so the gain is the signal, not the
extra training.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We formalize evolving-constraint dialogue as edit trajectories over a
  typed constraint state with tombstones, with executable metrics for
  persistence and relapse (the latter restricted to constraints whose
  chance-satisfaction rate is measured to be low), and show with a
  preregistered inference-only diagnostic that an 8B model fails on both
  and that prompting it to write its own state makes it worse.
- •
  We propose StateWise, a self-improving two-stage recipe with a
  verifiable round-trip filter and a relapse-contrastive preference
  stage, requiring no proprietary model and no human dialogue
  annotation, and we report the negative intermediate result that
  motivates the preference stage: tracking a state and obeying it are
  separable skills, and self-training with a filter teaches only the
  first.
- •
  Experiments on two backbones, held-out constraint families, unseen
  phrasings and public benchmarks, all under gates fixed before the
  runs, show relapse reductions of 8–22 points relative to supervised
  self-training and conversation-success gains of 8–19 points over the
  backbone; we also report the recipe’s cost on cumulative-constraint
  and single-turn benchmarks and show that weight interpolation with the
  backbone removes that cost at the price of the relapse gain, exposing
  a controllable trade-off.

## 2 Related Work

#### Multi-turn instruction following.

Multi-IF ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)), SysBench ([Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)), EvolIF ([Jia et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)) and
MultiTurnInstruct ([Han et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) document degradation
with dialogue depth, topic switches and revised goals;
conversational-reliability studies ([Laban et al., 2026](#bib.bib5))
show that sharding information over turns lowers accuracy. These are
evaluation resources. We use Multi-IF as a held-out test and add what it
lacks: constraints that are amended and withdrawn, with the relapse they
cause measured directly.

#### Verifiable instruction following.

IFEval ([Zhou et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)) introduced programmatic
checkers; IFBench ([Pyatkin et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)) added held-out
constraint families and showed that RLVR generalizes to them; [Ren
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib11) removed external supervision with constraint
decomposition and constraint-wise pseudo-labels. All train on
single-turn prompts. StateWise uses the same style of checkers but
trains on multi-turn edit trajectories with explicit state targets;
single-turn constraint training is one of our baselines, and we find
that it raises persistence and relapse together.

#### Lost in conversation and dialogue state.

RLAAR ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)) adds abstention rewards and a
curriculum for information revealed across turns; rolling-memory
policies compress fragmented history ([Luo et al., 2026](#bib.bib7));
history-cleaned self-distillation removes self-contamination ([Zheng
et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)). These address information fragmentation, not
constraint revision. Classic dialogue state tracking predicts slot
values over a fixed ontology for task-oriented systems ([Budzianowski
et al., 2018](#bib.bib1)); VLK-RL ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib16))
verifies LLM-elicited constraints for a separate RL policy. StateWise’s
state is an open set of executable constraint predicates with parameters
and tombstones, supervised by self-generated data, and lives in the same
model that responds.

#### Revocation inertia.

ReBIND ([Zhu, 2026](#bib.bib19)) measures per-clause influence in
code-generation dialogues and repairs relapse with an external compiled
ledger via the API alone. We adopt its tombstone semantics for ground
truth, train the model rather than wrap it, extend from code to general
formatting constraints, and compare against ReBIND-style compiled
ledgers as baselines, including a negative-priming variant that names
the withdrawn rules.

#### Self-improvement with round-trip filtering and preference signals.

SimRAG ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)) is the methodological template:
complementary skills, self-generated data and a consistency filter.
STaR-style rejection sampling ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib15)) and
self-instruct ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)) are the broader family;
self-rewarding and iterative DPO ([Yuan et al., 2024](#bib.bib14);
[Rafailov et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)) turn a model’s own judgments into
preference data. Our filter is exact match on a structured state plus
executable checks, not retrieval or LLM judgment, and our preference
pairs are labeled by the same checkers, so no judge model is involved in
the pipeline.

## 3 Problem Formulation

#### Constraints, edits and state.

A constraint is a pair $`c=(f,\theta)`$ of a family $`f`$ and parameters
$`\theta`$ with an executable checker
$`\mathrm{check}_{f}(y,\theta)\in\{0,1\}`$ over a response $`y`$;
examples are all*caps, max_words(80), end_phrase(“Is there anything
else?”), json_only and forbidden_word(“very”). Twelve families are used
in training and six further families appear only at test time
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Constraint Families and Trajectories ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")).
A dialogue applies one or more edits per user turn: add$`(c)`$,
amend$`(c\rightarrow c^{\prime})`$, revoke$`(c)`$, distract (an
unrelated request) and return (back to the task). The net state after
turn $`t`$ is $`S*{t}=(A*{t},R*{t})`$: the active set $`A*{t}`$ holds at
most one constraint per family, and the tombstone set $`R*{t}`$ holds
every revoked or superseded constraint. amend moves the old version to
$`R*{t}`$; re-adding a tombstoned constraint revives it. $`S*{t}`$ is
compiled from the edit list, has an order-independent canonical
serialization, and is therefore exact ground truth for both training and
evaluation at no annotation cost.

#### Metrics.

_Persistence_ at turn $`t`$ is the fraction of $`A_{t}`$ satisfied by
the response $`y_{t}`$. _Relapse_ at turn $`t`$ is the fraction of
$`R_{t}`$ satisfied by $`y_{t}`$, restricted to families whose
chance-satisfaction rate $`p_{0}\leq 0.10`$, where $`p_{0}`$ is measured
on the backbone’s own unconstrained responses to the same task prompts
(a response that happens to contain no commas is not evidence of relapse
for no_commas unless commas are otherwise common); an amended constraint
whose new version logically implies the old one is not counted.
_Conversation success_ requires every active constraint satisfied and
zero relapse at every turn. All metrics are averaged over conversations
and reported with conversation-level bootstrap intervals; comparisons
between arms are paired on shared trajectory identifiers.

#### Trajectory synthesis.

Scripted trajectories are generated from a seed: turn 0 adds one or two
constraints and requests a short task; later turns add, amend or revoke
with at most three constraints active and incompatible pairs (e.g.,
json_only with bullets_exact) never jointly active; half of the
trajectories insert a distract turn followed by a return; every
trajectory contains at least one revoke or amend; the final turn is
always a task turn. Each user message is composed from natural-language
phrasings of the edits plus a task prompt, so every assistant turn is
checkable. Trajectories have four to eight turns. Three evaluation sets
are used throughout: an in-distribution set (240 conversations, training
families and phrasings, unseen seed), a held-out set (300 conversations;
18 families of which 6 are never trained on), and a paraphrase set (300
conversations; author-written alternative phrasings and new task
prompts). Test sets are fixed before any training run.

## 4 Methodology

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Overview of StateWise. Stage I induces two complementary
skills from scripted trajectories whose ground-truth states are compiled
from the edit history. Stage II lets the model generate state and
response on fresh trajectories and keeps only turns that pass an exact
round-trip check. Stage III turns the same check into a preference
signal: the model’s relapsed generations are rejected responses, its
round-trip-clean generations are chosen responses. No proprietary model,
judge or human annotation is used in training.

### 4.1 Stage I: Skill Induction

Starting from an instruction-tuned backbone
(Figure [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")),
we fine-tune with LoRA on three mixtures built from scripted
trajectories
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")):
(a) single-turn verifiable instruction following, as in IFEval; (b)
_state summarization_, where the input is a dialogue prefix and the
target is the canonical JSON of the compiled state $`S_{t}`$, listing
active constraints with parameters and revoked constraints as
tombstones; and (c) _state-conditioned generation_, where the input is
the prefix plus the ground-truth state block and the target is a
response that passes every active checker, obtained by rejection
sampling from the backbone. Mixture sizes and hyper-parameters were
fixed before training
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training Details and Filter Statistics ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")).
Only the dialogue and the constraint library are needed; the backbone is
its own teacher.

### 4.2 Stage II: Self-Training with Round-Trip Filtering

The Stage-I model generates, for each turn of fresh trajectories, a
state block followed by a response. A turn is kept if and only if (i)
the emitted state equals the compiled state exactly, (ii) every active
checker passes, and (iii) no low-chance tombstoned constraint is
satisfied. Per-family shares are capped to avoid collapse onto easy
families. The model is fine-tuned on the kept turns (rejection-sampling
SFT). Filter yield and rejection reasons are in
Appendix [B](#A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Filter yields. ‣ Appendix B Training Details and Filter Statistics ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue");
on both backbones relapse is the dominant rejection reason,
foreshadowing
Section [6](#S6 "6 Experimental Results ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue"):
the filter removes relapsed examples but supplies no signal against
relapse.

### 4.3 Stage III: Relapse-Contrastive Preference Learning

The Stage-II model is sampled on a further set of trajectories (a
different seed from Stage II). For each turn we pair a _rejected_
response that enacts a tombstoned rule with a _chosen_ response from the
same prefix that passes the full round-trip check; a capped share (30%)
of pairs contrasts an active-constraint violation with a passing
response instead. The pairs are labeled entirely by the checkers and the
compiled state. We run DPO ([Rafailov et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)) with a
frozen reference (the Stage-II weights with adapters disabled),
$`\beta=0.1`$, an auxiliary NLL weight of 0.5 on the chosen response,
and a fixed budget of 59 optimizer steps over 931 pairs (947
constructed, 663 relapse and 284 active-violation, of which 16 were
dropped for length). Nothing is tuned after seeing results.

### 4.4 Inference

In _state mode_ the model emits its state block and then answers; the
block is stripped before the response is checked. In _state-free mode_
the same weights are prompted without the state instruction, which tests
whether the behavior is internalized. We also evaluate _weight
interpolation_
$`\theta_{\alpha}=\theta_{\text{base}}+\alpha(\theta_{\text{Stage III}}-\theta_{\text{base}})`$
for $`\alpha\in\{0.5,0.75\}`$, with no training, as a way to trade the
relapse gain against breadth on general instruction following
(Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 The Cost of Specialization and a Controllable Trade-Off ‣ 7 Analysis ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")).

## 5 Experimental Setup

#### Backbones and arms.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is the primary backbone (two training seeds) and
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct the secondary (one seed, full pipeline with Qwen as
its own teacher). The arms are: A0 the backbone; A1 single-turn
constraint training (rejection-sampling SFT on single-turn verifiable
prompts, the IFBench-style recipe); A2 Stage I only; A3 Stages I+II
without state supervision (same trajectories, checker-only filter); A4
Stages I+II with state (the self-training recipe); A5 A4 in state-free
mode; A9 Stage I with an active-only state block (no tombstones); A7 A4
plus Stage III (StateWise); and two ReBIND-style external-ledger
baselines around the untrained backbone at matched prompt tokens, A6,
which compiles the net specification including the withdrawn rules under
a “do not follow” header, and A6b, which lists only the rules in force.
A6b uses the compiled ground-truth state at inference and is therefore
an _oracle_ ledger.

#### Evaluation sets and metrics.

Held-out (300 conversations, 18 families, 6 unseen), in-distribution
(240 conversations) and paraphrase (300 conversations) sets
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")),
all with greedy decoding. Public benchmarks: Multi-IF ([He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib3), English, 909 conversations, prompt-level strict
accuracy at turns 1–3 with the model’s own history); IFEval ([Zhou
et al., 2023](#bib.bib18), 541 prompts, prompt-level strict and loose);
MT-Bench first-turn pairwise preference against the backbone judged by
gemma-2-9b-it in both presentation orders (a weak local judge;
regression signal only). Metrics are persistence, relapse and
conversation success
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")),
state exact-match for state-mode arms, and 95% conversation-level
bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples); deltas between arms are paired on
trajectory identifiers. The backbone’s own greedy results move by a few
points between runs because batched bf16 non-determinism compounds
across turns, so only within-run paired comparisons are used.

#### Preregistration.

Hypotheses, arms, metrics and pass/fail gates were fixed before each run
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Preregistration Summary ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue"))
and not changed after inspection; failed gates are reported as failures.
The main gates are G1 (A4 beats A0 on success and relapse), G2 (state
supervision helps: A4 vs. A3), H2 (gain survives state-free inference),
H3 (trained model matches the external ledger), H5 (Stage III beats A0
on success and relapse with intervals excluding zero), and, for the
extension, replication of direction on a second seed and backbone, a
Multi-IF direction check, a no-regression gate on IFEval (within 2
points), and two Stage-III ablation gates.

#### Training details.

LoRA rank 64, learning rate $`10^{-4}`$ for SFT stages; DPO as in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Methodology ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue").
Stage I uses 9.2k examples, Stage II the round-trip survivors of 2,400
self-generated trajectories (per-family caps), Stage III 931 pairs. Each
training run uses two A100-40GB GPUs; on Llama-3.1-8B, Stage I takes
about an hour, Stage II 68 minutes and Stage III 17 minutes. Full
hyper-parameters, data counts and filter statistics are in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training Details and Filter Statistics ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue").

## 6 Experimental Results

### 6.1 The Failure Exists and Prompting Does Not Fix It

Before training we ran a preregistered inference-only diagnostic on 240
trajectories (1,438 assistant turns) with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
(Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.1 The Failure Exists and Prompting Does Not Fix It ‣ 6 Experimental Results ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")).
Plain chat honors 79% of active constraints overall, falling from 0.887
at the first turn to 0.653 at the eighth, and enacts revoked low-chance
constraints on 11% of post-edit turns. A system prompt asking the model
to write its own constraint state before answering makes every metric
_worse_: persistence $`-0.21`$, relapse $`+0.05`$, success $`-0.19`$,
all with intervals excluding zero, and the emitted states match the
compiled ground truth 0.3% of the time (omitted rules, family
confusions, constraints hallucinated from task content, and an
always-empty revoked list). The failure is real at the 8B operating
point, prompting alone does not supply a usable state, and an external
ledger must therefore be compiled programmatically, as ReBIND does,
rather than requested from the model. This is the premise for training.

| Arm (no training)       | Persistence                   | Relapse                     | Conv. success                 | State match            |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Plain chat              | 0.793 \[0.767, 0.820\]        | 0.109 \[0.080, 0.141\]      | 0.275 \[0.225, 0.333\]        | –                      |
| State-scratchpad prompt | 0.587 \[0.547, 0.629\]        | 0.162 \[0.125, 0.200\]      | 0.088 \[0.054, 0.125\]        | 0.003 \[0.001, 0.006\] |
| Paired delta            | $`-0.206`$ \[-0.253, -0.160\] | $`+0.052`$ \[0.014, 0.090\] | $`-0.188`$ \[-0.250, -0.125\] |                        |

Table 1: Inference-only diagnostic (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, 240
conversations). Asking the untrained model to maintain its own
constraint state makes it worse on every metric.

Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6.2 Main Results ‣ 6 Experimental Results ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")
presents the preregistered arms on the primary backbone. From the
results, we have the following findings:

\(1\) _Every supervised arm learns to track the state and roughly
doubles relapse._ A4 emits the exact compiled state, tombstones
included, for 92% of in-distribution turns and raises persistence by
five points, yet its relapse is 0.246 held-out against the backbone’s
0.130 ($`+0.116`$ \[0.078, 0.151\], paired). The same doubling appears
without state supervision (A3, 0.277) and with an active-only state (A9,
0.276), and even single-turn constraint training raises relapse (A1,
0.164 from 0.130): making a model better at obeying constraints makes
withdrawn constraints stickier. State supervision helps only marginally
(A4 vs. A3: relapse $`-0.031`$ \[-0.058, -0.004\]), and the gain does
not survive removing the state at inference (A5). Under the
preregistered gates, G1, H2 and H3 fail and G2 passes narrowly. Tracking
the state and obeying it are separable skills, and rejection-sampling
SFT teaches the first without the second: the filter removes relapsed
examples but supplies no signal against relapse.

\(2\) _The relapse-contrastive stage supplies the missing signal._
Fifty-nine DPO steps on 931 self-generated contrasts cut relapse from
0.246 to 0.094 held-out ($`-0.152`$ \[-0.186, -0.120\]) and from 0.258
to 0.042 in distribution ($`-0.216`$ \[-0.258, -0.177\]), to below the
backbone ($`-0.036`$ \[-0.065, -0.011\] held-out; $`-0.068`$ \[-0.099,
-0.040\] in-dist.) while keeping the persistence gain ($`+0.035`$
\[0.002, 0.067\] over A0) and lifting conversation success ($`+0.080`$
\[0.020, 0.140\] held-out; $`+0.279`$ \[0.204, 0.350\] in-dist.). State
exact-match is unchanged (0.893 vs. 0.916 in-dist.): the gain is in
obeying the state, not in tracking it. Gate H5 passes.

\(3\) _StateWise matches or beats an oracle external ledger without
scaffolding._ A6b, the untrained backbone wrapped in a programmatically
compiled active-only ledger with ground-truth knowledge of every edit,
is the strongest baseline. StateWise is below it on relapse everywhere
($`-0.054`$ \[-0.081, -0.030\] held-out; $`-0.042`$ \[-0.070, -0.017\]
in-dist.), matches it on held-out success ($`-0.020`$ \[-0.080, 0.043\])
and beats it in distribution ($`+0.092`$ \[0.029, 0.158\]); the
remaining gap is four points of persistence. The ledger variant that
names withdrawn rules under a “do not follow” header (A6) nearly triples
relapse (0.380): any salient mention of a revoked rule, even negated,
primes the 8B model to enact it. This priming does not transfer to a
trained self-emitted state: A9, whose state block omits the tombstones,
relapses no less than A2, which names them ($`+0.022`$ \[-0.004,
0.051\]).

and pair pool as A7; preregistered). Pair counts are before length

(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training Details and Filter Statistics ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")).

varies only the preference pairs. _Label-shuffled pairs do nothing_:
A7-shuf is indistinguishable from A4 on every metric (relapse $`-0.004`$

### 7.2 The Cost of Specialization and a Controllable Trade-Off

|                               | Held-out (ours) |         |          | IFEval |       | Multi-IF (prompt-strict) |       |       |
| ----------------------------- | --------------- | ------- | -------- | ------ | ----- | ------------------------ | ----- | ----- |
| Model                         | Success         | Relapse | Persist. | strict | loose | T1                       | T2    | T3    |
| A0 backbone                   | 0.290           | 0.130   | 0.799    | 0.725  | 0.771 | 0.735                    | 0.557 | 0.400 |
| A6b oracle ledger             | 0.390           | 0.148   | 0.877    | –      | –     | –                        | –     | –     |
| A4 self-training              | 0.327           | 0.246   | 0.853    | 0.667  | 0.697 | 0.702                    | 0.508 | 0.351 |
| A7 StateWise ($`\alpha=1`$)   | 0.370           | 0.094   | 0.834    | 0.660  | 0.686 | 0.678                    | 0.496 | 0.336 |
| A7, state-free inference      | –               | –       | –        | 0.636  | 0.689 | –                        | –     | –     |
| interpolation $`\alpha=0.75`$ | 0.397           | 0.125   | 0.857    | 0.686  | 0.723 | 0.695                    | 0.516 | 0.374 |
| interpolation $`\alpha=0.5`$  | 0.413           | 0.152   | 0.885    | 0.706  | 0.728 | 0.725                    | 0.560 | 0.407 |

Table 5: Breadth. Multi-IF (909 English conversations) accumulates
constraints without ever revoking them; IFEval (541 prompts) is
single-turn.
$`\theta_{\alpha}=\theta_{\text{base}}+\alpha(\theta_{\textsc{A7}}-\theta_{\text{base}})`$
with no training; both $`\alpha`$ values were fixed in advance.

Specializing an 8B model to revocable formatting constraints from a
12-family library costs breadth
(Table [5](#S7.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 7.2 The Cost of Specialization and a Controllable Trade-Off ‣ 7 Analysis ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")).
On Multi-IF, where constraints only accumulate and most of IFEval’s 25
instruction types are outside our training families, the trained arms
are worse than the backbone at every turn (A7: $`-6.5`$ points at turn
3), and on single-turn IFEval A7 is $`6.5`$ points below the backbone on
prompt-strict accuracy, failing the preregistered 2-point no-regression
gate; a weak pairwise judge on MT-Bench first turns sees a small
regression (win 5%, tie 80%, loss 15%). This is a real cost, not a
tooling artifact, and we report it as such.

Weight interpolation with the backbone exposes the trade-off as a single
knob. At $`\alpha=0.5`$ the model is within 1.9 points of the backbone
on IFEval and, on Multi-IF, within one point of it at turn 1 and above
it at turns 2–3 ($`+0.7`$ at turn 3), while having the highest
conversation success (0.413, $`+0.123`$ \[0.057, 0.187\] over A0) and
persistence ($`+0.087`$ \[0.059, 0.114\]) of any arm and matching the
oracle ledger on every held-out metric (success $`+0.023`$ \[-0.037,
0.083\], relapse $`+0.004`$ \[-0.023, 0.031\]). What it gives back is
the relapse gain: relapse returns to the backbone level ($`+0.022`$
\[-0.007, 0.051\]). The preregistered interpolation gate—IFEval within 2
points _and_ relapse below the backbone with an interval excluding
zero—is therefore not met by either $`\alpha`$, and we do not select an
$`\alpha`$ post hoc. The honest summary is a Pareto frontier:
$`\alpha=1`$ for the lowest relapse, $`\alpha=0.5`$ for the broadest
model that still tracks its state, with the untested mitigation being to
mix general instruction data into Stages I–III so that the frontier
itself moves.

### 7.3 Where the Relapse Goes

Per-turn curves
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Results ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue"))
show that the backbone’s persistence declines monotonically with depth
while relapse is flat at 0.09–0.13 on every post-edit turn; A4 lifts
persistence at all depths and lifts relapse in the same way, and A7
keeps the persistence curve while pulling relapse below the backbone at
every depth. By family, relapse concentrates on constraints that are
easy to keep enacting silently once learned—no_commas, no_digits,
sentence_count, paragraphs_exact—and Stage III removes most of it
without touching the state block (state exact-match is unchanged), which
is the behavioral signature of a model that knew the rule was withdrawn
and had not been told that this mattered.

## 8 Conclusion

Evolving-constraint dialogue exposes two failures in instruction-tuned
LLMs, forgetting active constraints and re-enacting withdrawn ones, and
the only prior repair we are aware of wraps the model in an external
ledger. We showed that a SimRAG-style self-improvement recipe with an
exact round-trip filter teaches a 7–8B model to track its own constraint
state almost perfectly without teaching it to obey that state: on
Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse, and on
Qwen2.5-7B none reduces it. Tracking and obeying are separable skills,
and a filter can only teach the first. Turning the same verifiable check
into a preference signal supplies what the filter cannot, a negative
signal against relapse, and 59 steps of DPO on self-labeled contrasts
cut relapse by 8–22 points, below the backbone and below an oracle
compiled ledger, on two backbones, two seeds and unseen phrasings, with
ablations that isolate the relapse-specific contrast as the necessary
ingredient. The recipe costs breadth on cumulative-constraint and
single-turn benchmarks, and interpolating with the backbone trades that
cost against the relapse gain along a single knob. Every number on our
evaluation sets comes from executable checkers against compiled states,
and training uses no proprietary model, judge or human dialogue
annotation; the only judge-based number is the MT-Bench regression
signal.

## 9 Limitations

Constraint families are formatting-level and programmatically checkable,
and trajectories are scripted from templates with a paraphrase set as
the only test of phrasing shift; semantic constraints and user phrasings
in the wild are broader. The relapse metric excludes high-chance
families by construction and therefore understates relapse on
constraints that are easy to satisfy accidentally. Results are for 7–8B
backbones with LoRA; stronger models may sit near the floor on relapse,
as ReBIND reports, and the breadth cost may differ. The held-out success
intervals have half-widths of about five points, and relapse relative to
the backbone crosses zero on one seed and touches it on the paraphrase
set. The specialization cost on Multi-IF and IFEval is real, the
interpolation remedy removes it only by giving back the relapse gain,
and the obvious mitigation of mixing general instruction data into
training was not run. The MT-Bench judge is a weak local model and its
signal is indicative only.

### AI use statement

Large language models were used as writing and coding assistants: to
draft and edit prose, to write and refactor training, evaluation and
analysis scripts, to format and check references, and to port the
manuscript into this template. The hypotheses, preregistered gates,
experimental design and interpretation are the authors’; all reported
numbers are produced by the released code from result artifacts and were
checked by the authors against those artifacts; LLM-generated code was
tested before use. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work and take
responsibility for the final content of this work, including text,
claims and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

### Reproducibility statement

Backbones (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and benchmarks
(Multi-IF, IFEval, MT-Bench) are public. The constraint library,
trajectory generator, checkers, state compiler, round-trip filter, pair
construction, training configurations and evaluation scripts will be
released together with every result JSON (each with a configuration
snapshot and content hash), the fixed test-set seeds
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")),
the preregistered protocol with its amendments
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Preregistration Summary ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")),
and the exact hyper-parameters
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training Details and Filter Statistics ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue")).
Because Python’s random sequences can differ across interpreter
versions, the generated trajectories are stored alongside the results.

## Appendix A Constraint Families and Trajectories

Training families (12): all*caps, all_lower, no_commas, end_phrase,
start_phrase, keyword_count, json_only, bullets_exact, max_words,
forbidden_word, paragraphs_exact, wrap_quotes. Held-out families (6,
test only): no_digits, sentence_count, title_brackets, postscript,
two_responses, numbered_sections. Each family has an executable checker
and one to three natural-language phrasings per operation (add, amend,
revoke); the paraphrase set uses three further author-written phrasings
per family and operation and new task prompts. Measured
chance-satisfaction rates $`p*{0}`$ on the backbone’s unconstrained
responses are below 0.05 for every family except forbidden_word
(0.94–0.95), which is therefore excluded from relapse, and
paragraphs_exact (0.04) and bullets_exact (0.02), which are retained.
Trajectories are generated from a seed with 4–8 turns, at most three
active constraints, incompatible pairs never jointly active, a
distract/return pair in half of the trajectories, and at least one
revoke or amend per trajectory. Test sets: held-out seed 777 (300
conversations), in-distribution seed 20260916 (240), paraphrase seed 999
(300); training trajectories use disjoint seeds.

## Appendix B Training Details and Filter Statistics

#### SFT stages.

LoRA rank 64, $`\alpha=128`$, dropout 0.05 on all attention and MLP
projections; learning rate $`10^{-4}`$, 3% warm-up, one epoch, effective
batch 16 sequences, maximum length 4,096; identical for every SFT arm,
only the data differs. Stage I (Llama): 9,238 examples, 578 steps, 55–61
minutes on two A100s (loss 0.29 $`\rightarrow`$ 0.07 for the state arm).
Stage II (state arm): 9,920 kept turns, 620 steps, 68 minutes.
Single-turn arm A1: 2,237 examples, 140 steps.

#### Stage III (DPO).

Base and frozen reference: the Stage-II state model; LoRA as above;
learning rate $`2\times 10^{-5}`$, 5% warm-up, one epoch, effective
batch 16 pairs, $`\beta=0.1`$, NLL weight 0.5 on the chosen response, at
most 30% active-violation pairs. 931 pairs encoded (663 relapse, 284
active-violation; 16 dropped for length), 59 steps, 17 minutes; training
preference accuracy 0.50 $`\rightarrow`$ 1.00 and loss 0.77
$`\rightarrow`$ 0.31. Ablations: relapse-only 649 pairs / 41 steps;
active-only 922 pairs / 58 steps; label-shuffled 931 pairs / 59 steps.
All values were fixed in the protocol amendment of 2026-09-16 16:50 and
never tuned.

#### Filter yields.

A turn is rejected when none of its $`K=4`$ sampled candidates passes,
which also stops the trajectory; a rejected turn is counted under every
distinct reason among its candidates, so reason counts slightly exceed
rejected-turn counts. Stage-I data generation (backbone as teacher, 4
shards): 10,723 turns attempted, 9,238 kept (yield 0.86); stopping
reasons 485 active-constraint violations vs. 1,027 relapses. Stage-II
generation with the state model: 11,243 attempted, 9,920 kept (0.88);
reasons 411 active violations, 887 relapses, 158 state mismatches.
Relapse is the dominant rejection reason at every stage and on both
backbones (Qwen Stage I: 1,253 relapse vs. 446 active-violation stops),
which is the data-side signature of the result in
Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Main Results ‣ 6 Experimental Results ‣ StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue").

#### Per-turn behavior.

#### Prompts.

The state-mode system prompt asks the model to begin its reply with a
fenced JSON block containing active (list of {family, params}) and
revoked (same schema) and then to answer; the block is stripped before
checking. State-free mode uses the backbone’s default system prompt. The
ledger baselines prepend the compiled specification (A6b: rules in
force; A6: rules in force plus a “do not follow” list of withdrawn
rules) to every user turn, matched in token count to the state block.
